newsitem.title: VATICAN: Pope to urge reconciliation on visit to Sarajevo.
newsitem.headline: Pope to urge reconciliation on visit to Sarajevo.

text.p: Pope John Paul will make a strong appeal for peace and reconciliation at the weekend when he pays a historic visit to Sarajevo, scarred by a war driven by ethnic and religious hatreds.
His 25-hour visit to the Bosnian capital, now a mainly Moslem city, is one of the most emotional in recent years of a papacy dogged by declining health and advancing age.

It comes at a time of tensions in the shaky federation between Roman Catholic Croats and Moslems, with little sign that the ethnic separation wrought by their conflict and their war with Orthodox Serbs has been diminished by peace.

"As Successor of Peter, I am going to confirm in faith our brothers and sisters in a city which, in a certain sense, has become a sad symbol of the tragedies which have struck Europe in the 20th century," the Pope said on Wednesday.
"May this Apostolic Visit also become a voyage of peace on which the Church bears witness to its solidarity with suffering men and peoples," he said at his weekly general audience.

Fears for the 76-year-old Pope's security have been fuelled by a wave of attacks on churches and mosques over the past two months. A monastery and a church in central Sarajevo were among the targets of the attacks, none of which caused injuries.
Authorities in the capital say they will deploy thousands of local police for the visit. United Nations police and NATO forces have said they will provide support.
The Bosnian conflict and the Serb siege of Sarajevo, both halted by the Dayton peace deal in late 1995, were constant themes of the Polish-born Pope's addresses for much of the past four years.
During the war, he condemned religious bigotry and nationalism and since the peace has frequently urged Croats, Moslems and Bosnian Serbs to rebuild co-existence.

"The Pope is the symbol of reconciliation and understanding and in few places is that message as important and as necessary as in Sarajevo," the international community's High Representative in Bosnia, Carl Bildt, said earlier this year.

In 1995 the Pope appeared to weep publicly over the suffering in Bosnia and in 1994, on a visit to overwhelmingly Catholic Croatia, he condemned ultra-nationalism and the use of religion to justify the wars that tore apart former Yugoslavia.
"No, it is not lawful to attribute to religion the phenomenon of nationalistic intolerance which is raging in this region," the Pope said in Zagreb.
He had planned to visit Sarajevo the same year, while war was still raging, but cancelled the trip when Bosnian Serbs besieging the city said they could not guarantee his safety.
Orthodox Serbs have long regarded the Pope as hostile to them, following early Vatican recognition of Croatian independence.
This time, however, the visit has the support of all three members of Bosnia-Herzegovina's new collective presidency, including Serb representative Momcilo Krajisnik.

The population of Sarajevo, former Yugoslavia's most cosmopolitan city, has become predominantly Moslem with the departure of Serbs from suburbs their forces controlled during the war and assigned by Dayton to the Moslem-Croat Federation.

The main public event of the Pope's visit will be an open-air mass on Sunday at Kosevo soccer stadium, repaired after war damage. The Pope was also due to meet Bosnian leaders and representatives of other religious groups.

It was not clear who would attend but the Vatican said this week that the Pope would use the occasion to make donations of $50,000 each to humanitarian organisations from the Catholic, Moslem, Serb Orthodox and Jewish faiths.

The trip is the Pope's first since an appendix operation last October since when he has cut back on some of his public engagements. He is due to go later this month to Prague and also has trips this year to Lebanon, Poland, France and Brazil.
